titel: Partial exemption and advance lump sum
kurz: Why income from an equity ETF is taxed at only 18.46%, and why the bank still debits money from the settlement account in January.

bloecke.md:
Until the end of 2017, a fund paid no tax itself; for tax purposes, its income was attributed in full to the investor. This worked as long as the fund was set up in Germany and properly reported its income on the annual certificate. It did not work for foreign accumulating funds. Their income often remained untaxed for decades, and investors who wanted to declare it correctly had to search laboriously for the figures in the Federal Gazette (Bundesanzeiger).

On 1 January 2018, this system was replaced. Since then, the fund itself has paid tax on part of its income, and in return the investor receives a flat-rate relief. At the same time, an annual minimum taxation was introduced so that tax can no longer be deferred indefinitely. These two rules, the [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]] and the [[Advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)|advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)]], are the reason why the tax certificate for an ETF portfolio looks different from that for a share portfolio.

## Purpose of the partial exemption

Under Sections 6 and 7 InvStG (Investment Tax Act), since 2018 a fund has itself paid 15% corporation tax on three types of domestic income: dividends from German public limited companies, domestic real estate income and other domestic income. For income subject to tax deduction, above all dividends, the solidarity surcharge is already included in this 15%. For assessed income such as domestic rents, it is added on top, making 15.825% in total there. This tax does not appear on the investor's statements; it reduces the unit price.

If the investor then also had to pay the full flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) on the same income, they would be taxed twice. The partial exemption under Section 20 InvStG compensates for this on a flat-rate basis by leaving a fixed percentage of the income tax-free for the investor. It is therefore a balancing mechanism within the tax system, neither a loophole nor a subsidy. That is why it is zero for bond funds, because their interest income is not taxed in advance at fund level.

bloecke.titel: Three special cases of the partial exemption
bloecke.md:
If the investment terms contain no commitment to a minimum ratio, the bank applies a 0% partial exemption when deducting tax, even if the ETF in fact holds 100% shares. In practice, this affects certain swap-based and special structures. If the investor proves that the fund exceeded the ratio throughout the calendar year, they receive the partial exemption on application in the tax return (Section 20(4) InvStG). The rate applied is stated in the provider's tax information, not in the factsheet.

The partial exemption also applies to losses. If an equity fund is in the red, only 70% of the loss can be offset; the remaining 30% is disregarded for tax purposes. The same rule that provides relief in the case of a gain therefore reduces the amount that can be offset in the case of a loss.

Commodities and gold are not covered. Commodity ETCs and physically backed gold ETCs are usually not investment funds within the meaning of the InvStG at all and follow their own rules. Bond funds and money market funds are funds, but their partial exemption rate is zero.

## Order of the calculation

The tax is calculated in three steps, and their order is fixed. First, the partial exemption is deducted from the gross income. Then the [[Saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag)|saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag)]] of €1,000 under Section 20(9) EStG (Income Tax Act) is taken into account, or €2,000 for joint assessment. Only the remaining amount is subject to 25% capital income withholding tax (Kapitalertragsteuer) plus a 5.5% [[Solidarity surcharge|solidarity surcharge]], 26.375% in total.

If the allowance has already been used up elsewhere, the effective tax on income from an equity fund is 0.70 × 26.375 = 18.46% instead of 26.375%. With 9% church tax, it is around 19.60% instead of 27.995%. The difference is large enough to be taken into account when choosing between a bond ETF and a mixed fund. However, it must never be the sole reason for an investment decision; it is only one factor in the after-tax calculation.

bloecke.md:
## Purpose of the advance lump sum

The partial exemption lowers the tax permanently; the advance lump sum under Section 18 InvStG brings it forward in time. For accumulating funds and funds that distribute too little, it taxes a notional minimum return every year. This is intended to prevent an investor from building up wealth completely tax-free for thirty years, while a direct investor in shares pays tax on their dividends every year.

bloecke.formel:
Base return = Redemption price on 1 January × Base interest rate × 0.7

Advance lump sum = Base return − Distributions for the year

Cap = Increase in value for the year (last minus first
      redemption price) + Distributions

In the year of purchase: × (12 − full months before the month of purchase) / 12
bloecke.erklaerung: The factor 0.7 is a statutory flat-rate cost deduction. It is applied to the base interest rate (Basiszins), not to the increase in value. The cap is the full increase in value, not 70% of it. This confusion is found in many online guides.
variablen: determined by the Bundesbank from the yield curve for public bonds with a remaining maturity of 15 years as of the first trading day of the year, and published by the Federal Ministry of Finance (BMF) in the Federal Tax Gazette (Section 18(4) InvStG)
unit value determined by the fund management company, not the ETF's stock exchange price
bloecke.beispiel: In 2026, the base return (Basisertrag) is 3.20% base interest rate × 0.7 = 2.24% of the fund value at the start of the year.

bloecke.md:
The rise from 2022 to 2023 is the main reason why the advance lump sum only became an issue in Germany late on. In the first five years, the annual charge on an equity ETF portfolio ranged from cents to low euro amounts, and in two of those years it was zero. Since 2023, it has been clearly noticeable in the settlement account, and in 2026 the base interest rate, at 3.20%, reached its highest level since the rule was introduced.

The advance lump sum for a year is only deemed received on the first working day of the following year (Section 18(3) InvStG). The base interest rate of 3.20% therefore relates to 2026, but the tax on the advance lump sum calculated from it is only debited in January 2027.

bloecke.titel: Cost of the advance lump sum per €10,000 in an equity ETF

bloecke.md:
The value of an accumulating equity ETF with a 30% partial exemption rises from €30,000 on 1 January 2026 to €34,000 on 31 December 2026. The saver's allowance has already been used up elsewhere.

- Base return: €30,000 × 3.20% × 0.7 = €672.00
- The increase in value of €4,000 is considerably higher, so the cap does not apply.
- The advance lump sum is therefore €672.00.
- After the 30% partial exemption (€201.60 tax-free), €470.40 is taxable.
- Tax: €470.40 × 26.375% = €124.068, or €124.06 after rounding the solidarity surcharge down to whole cents

That is around 0.41% of the portfolio value. The bank debits the amount in the first days of January 2027, without the investor having received any money.

bloecke.titel: Cap on the advance lump sum for five different performances
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with a fund value of €30,000 at the start of the year and a base interest rate of 3.20%. The base return is the same in all cases; the advance lump sum is capped at the increase in value in the year concerned.

bloecke.md:
## Crediting distributions

The advance lump sum also affects distributing funds. It is the difference between the base return and the distributions for the year. If the distribution is below the base return, a remainder is left.

Two ETFs on the same index are each worth €30,000 on 1 January 2026 and perform identically. One accumulates in full; the other distributes €540 (1.8%). For the accumulating ETF, the advance lump sum is €672; for the distributing one, it is 672 − 540 = €132. The first incurs €124.06 of tax on the advance lump sum. For the second, it is €99.69 on the distribution plus €24.37 on the advance lump sum, so also €124.06 in total, to the cent.

A difference only arises if the distribution exceeds the base return or is higher than the entire performance for the year, for example in a loss-making year. In that case no advance lump sum is due, but the full distribution is taxable, and more tax falls due on the distributing fund. Since the reform, the difference between [[Accumulation|accumulation]] and distribution has thus been limited to the remainder between the performance achieved and the capped base return, the taxation of which is deferred until the sale.

With the advance lump sum, tax falls due without the investor receiving any money. The custodian bank collects the tax automatically from the settlement account in the first days of January. If the balance is insufficient, it draws on a linked current account or instant-access savings account, asks for a deposit or reports the matter to the tax office (Section 44(1) sentences 7 to 11 EStG). Some providers sell fund units for this purpose.

The timing of the exemption order also plays a role. The advance lump sum belongs to the capital income of the year in which it is deemed received. An [[Exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag)|exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag)]] that is only issued in February therefore also covers the January debit. By then, however, the bank has already debited the tax and must refund it as long as it has not yet issued the tax certificate for the year (Section 44b(5) EStG). If the order is already in place before the turn of the year, the bank does not debit any tax in the first place, up to the amount of the order.

## Offsetting on sale

The most common misconception is to regard the advance lump sum as an additional tax. It is an advance payment. Under Section 19(1) InvStG, the capital gain on sale is reduced by all advance lump sums assessed during the holding period, in full and without any reduction for the partial exemption. As a result, the tax office ultimately receives exactly the same amount as it would without the advance lump sum.

The units are bought in 2026 for €30,000 and sold in 2031 for €50,000. Over the holding period, advance lump sums totalling €3,200 were assessed. This figure is an assumption, because future base interest rates have not yet been set.

| Step | Amount |
|---|---|
| Raw gain | €20,000.00 |
| Less advance lump sums assessed (Section 19(1) InvStG) | −€3,200.00 |
| Capital gain | €16,800.00 |
| After deducting the 30% partial exemption | €11,760.00 |
| Tax on sale (26.375%) | €3,101.70 |
| Already paid during the holding period (€3,200 × 0.7 × 26.375%) | €590.80 |
| Total | €3,692.50 |

Without the advance lump sum, the result would be €20,000 × 0.7 × 26.375% = €3,692.50, the same amount. The only difference lies in the timing of the payment and thus in the compound interest forgone on the amounts paid early.

The partial exemption determines how much tax is due; the advance lump sum only determines when it is paid. Anyone who confuses the two regards the January debit as an extra burden on accumulating funds. It is, however, a down payment that is credited to the cent on sale.

The former grandfathering for units acquired before 1 January 2009 was limited by the reform. Under Section 56(2) InvStG, all fund units are deemed to have been sold on 31 December 2017 and newly acquired on 1 January 2018. The last redemption price set in 2017 is decisive. For genuine old units, the increases in value up to that date remain tax-free; all later ones are taxable.

In return, there is a personal allowance of €100,000 on the increases in value accrued from 2018 onwards (Section 56(6) InvStG). The bank does not take it into account. It is only granted in the assessment procedure, determined separately each year and used up gradually. Investors with old holdings who do not file a tax return therefore do not receive it.

Two judgments of the Federal Fiscal Court (BFH) of 25 November 2025 (VIII R 15/22 and VIII R 22/23) concern units bought between 2009 and 2017. According to these, the partial exemption is not to be applied to the extent that a capital loss arises solely because the notional acquisition costs as of 1 January 2018 are higher than the historical ones. As of September 2026, it had not been conclusively clarified whether the tax authorities will apply the judgments generally.

1. Before the turn of the year, leave roughly 0.5% of the value of your fund holdings in the settlement account as a reserve. With €100,000 in an equity ETF, the tax on the advance lump sum is around €414 based on the 2026 figures.
2. Check the exemption order before New Year's Eve. It also applies to the advance lump sum. If it is already in place when the January debit is made, the advance lump sum remains tax-free up to the amount of the order; an order issued later in the same year leads to a refund by the bank.
3. Look up the partial exemption rate. It is stated in the provider's tax information or prospectus, not in the factsheet. For bond and money market ETFs, it is zero.
4. With foreign brokers, do the calculation yourself. Without German tax deduction, the advance lump sum and partial exemption must be declared in the investment fund income annex (Anlage KAP-INV), because nobody debits anything there.

mitnehmen: The partial exemption compensates on a flat-rate basis for the fact that, since 2018, the fund itself has paid 15% corporation tax on domestic dividends and real estate income.

For tax deduction, only the ratio commitment in the investment terms counts, not the composition of the portfolio; an equity ETF without such a commitment only receives the partial exemption on application in the tax return if the ratio was demonstrably exceeded throughout the year.
The base return is the fund value on 1 January × base interest rate × 0.7, and the advance lump sum is this amount less distributions, but at most the increase in value for the year.
The base interest rate for 2026 is 3.20%, but the tax on the resulting advance lump sum is only debited automatically in January 2027, without any money being received.
On sale, all advance lump sums assessed are deducted in full from the gain, so that the same tax is due overall, only partly earlier.

begriffe.text: Flat-rate tax-free portion of income from investment funds under Section 20 InvStG. For private assets, it is 30% for equity funds, 15% for mixed funds, 60% or 80% for real estate funds and 0% for bond and money market funds. The partial exemption compensates for the tax already paid at fund level and also applies to losses.

Notional minimum return of accumulating or low-distributing funds that is taxed every year (Section 18 InvStG). It is capped at the increase in value, falls due on the first working day of the following year and is credited in full on sale.

Redemption price of the fund unit at the start of the year, multiplied by 70% of the base interest rate. It is the starting figure for the advance lump sum, and the reduction to 70% is a statutory cost deduction.

Share of equities and comparable holdings that a fund's investment terms commit to on a continuous basis. Above 50%, the fund counts as an equity fund; at 25% or more, as a mixed fund (Section 2(6) and (7) InvStG).
